title: Twelve baskets left (John 6:1–15)
hook: gather the fragments so nothing is lost

segments.voice: Yesterday, four witnesses, and the last was a book. Your line was the scriptures point to him.

A crowd on a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee, about five thousand men, John says. Passover is near, the feast that remembers the night Israel left Egypt. Jesus asks Philip, as a test: where shall we buy bread for all these? Philip does the math and gives up: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little." Not even a little each. Then Andrew notices a boy.

Andrew says: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Matthew, Mark and Luke tell this story too, but John is the one who mentions the boy, and that the loaves were barley. A kid's lunch, offered to a crowd. Jesus has everyone sit on the grass. He takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Everyone eats until full. The Gospels don't describe how it happened, only what people saw: enough. Then the part this day is named for: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." The disciples go around the hillside collecting broken pieces, and fill twelve baskets. A miracle has just happened, and the next thing Jesus cares about is the crumbs. Twelve baskets: one for each disciple doing the gathering, maybe, or a number some readers connect with the twelve tribes of Israel. All four Gospels tell this feeding, and some Christians hear in it the Lord's Supper too: he took bread, gave thanks, and gave it. And the scene ends strangely. The crowd wants to seize Jesus and make him king by force. He slips away alone, up the mountain. He came to feed them, not to be crowned by them.

Picture your kitchen, half a loaf, a few vegetables, last night's rice, and find one thing that might get thrown out that you could use. Then widen it: a half-finished letter, an hour you usually waste, a small skill nobody asks for. If you pray, give thanks for what's already there, the way Jesus gave thanks over a boy's lunch; if you don't, simply notice how much is there.
Fragments. What the disciples gathered after five thousand ate, so that nothing would be lost: twelve baskets of broken pieces.
Your line: let nothing be lost. Even the crumbs count, all twelve baskets of them. Rest well.

howItsDone: Some Christians give thanks before meals, as Jesus does here, and some churches run food banks and community meals, gathering surplus food so nothing is wasted.

original.note: Greek: broken pieces, fragments. The word for what was left over.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a miracle of lots of food.
what it means: a boy's small lunch becomes enough, and Jesus makes sure even the crumbs aren't wasted.
what a scholar hears: John sets the scene near Passover, and some readers hear echoes of manna in the desert and of the Lord's Supper in "took, gave thanks, gave."

the five loaves the boy gave before the meal

chat.says: After feeding all those people, why did Jesus care about the leftovers?
options: He said gather the fragments, that nothing be lost: twelve baskets, nothing wasted.
He wanted the scraps thrown away so nobody could prove a miracle happened.
He saved them to sell in town and pay back the two hundred pennyworth.
chat.meaning: Right after the miracle, Jesus said: gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost. They filled twelve baskets.

Passover.meaning: the feast remembering the night Israel left Egypt

pennyworth.meaning: old money word: two hundred wouldn't buy enough bread

Sea of Galilee.meaning: the lake beside the hillside where the crowd sat

twelve tribes of Israel.meaning: the twelve family lines of ancient Israel

Lord's Supper.meaning: the Christian meal of bread and wine, also called communion

sources.quoted: Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little.
There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?

notes: KJV 'penny' = denarius, a day's wage (cf. Matthew 20:2). Confirm.
Barley bread as the cheaper bread of the poor: common commentary claim. Confirm.
'The only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that all four Gospels tell': common claim; confirm.
Twelve baskets linked to twelve disciples or twelve tribes: given as readings, not fact.
The script says the Gospels don't describe how the multiplication happened; confirm wording is acceptable across churches.

Editor review (2026-10-01): fixed the hook's claim that Passover remembers manna in the desert (Passover remembers the exodus; manna is Exodus 16); 'five thousand people' now follows John 6:10 ('about five thousand' men); cut the unsourced 'a penny is a day's wage', 'barley, the bread of poor families' and 'the only miracle besides the resurrection that all four tell' (teach, match, myth); 'only John' softened to 'John is the one who mentions'; 'many readers' and 'many Christians' softened. Keeper: confirm the boy and the barley are absent from Matthew 14, Mark 6 and Luke 9.
